contract explicitly, irrevocably, and unambiguously designates the roof as a "Limited Common 
Element for Unit 2's exclusive use".1 Under New York Real Property Law (RPL § 339-i) and 
binding First Department precedent, "exclusive means exclusive" regarding limited common 
elements.1 Therefore, pleading that Unit 1 held a 25% economic interest in the roof's FAR was a 
direct, fabricated factual misrepresentation designed to deceive the Court into granting an 
injunction, perfectly satisfying the scienter requirement of Judiciary Law § 487.1 
Fraud Upon the Tribunal: Concealment of CofO Violations 
A preliminary injunction is governed by the equitable maxim that a party must come to the 
court with "clean hands".1 Injunctive relief is absolutely barred if the proponent is guilty of 
unlawful conduct directly related to the litigation.1 To bypass this requirement, Giacovas 
systematically concealed his clients' own severe municipal violations to manipulate the "judicial 
balance of equities".1 
On January 17, 2025, Justice Mary V. Rosado issued a preliminary injunction enjoining Damerau 
from removing the HVAC unit based on Giacovas's portrayal of the Bleichs as vulnerable 
homeowners facing the inequitable loss of winter heating.1 However, Giacovas deliberately 
concealed that Unit 1 was actively operating in severe violation of the building's Certificate of 
Occupancy (CofO) by maintaining an unlicensed, legally noncompliant cellar space containing 
unlawful bedrooms and bathrooms.1 
By demanding the Supreme Court force the Condominium Board to tolerate Bleich's 
unpermitted rooftop HVAC unit—an action that legally forces the Board into a dereliction of its 
fiduciary duty to cure municipal violations—while simultaneously hiding Bleich's own active, 
severe CofO violations, Giacovas committed fraud upon the tribunal.1 
Collateral Estoppel and the Resurrection of Defeated Theories 
The bad-faith posture is further evidenced by the resurrection of legally frivolous arguments.1 
In a prior 2019 lawsuit (13 Harrison St. Condominium v Bleich, Index No. 651188/19), the Board 
sued Bleich over the illegal cellar alterations.1 Bleich argued that because the New York City 
Department of Buildings (DOB) had never formally issued a fine, the alterations were legally 
permissible.1 On May 24, 2022, the Appellate Division, First Department, resoundingly rejected 
this defense, explicitly ruling that the mere absence of DOB fines does not establish 
compliance with a certificate of occupancy.1 
Despite this binding appellate precedent between the exact same parties, Giacovas 
resurrected the identical legal theory in the 2024 HVAC dispute.1 He successfully argued to the 
trial court that because the Board had allowed the unpermitted HVAC to remain on the roof 
"for over a decade" without fines, the Board had waived its right to remove it.1 Asserting legal 
theories explicitly rejected by appellate courts in the same context constitutes legally frivolous
